headlines.title: Saudi Aramco headquarters suffered extensive damage in Houthi attack, sources say - Reuters
headlines.summary: One, the Houthis hit Saudi Aramco's actual headquarters (not a pipeline somewhere in the desert — the headquarters, in Dhahran, which is a bit like bombing the lobby of a company you're mad at), and two, they then vowed more attacks on airports and oil facilities, which is the kind of follow-up statement that tends to make crude oil futures do something dramatic before breakfast. This hits energy broadly (USO, XLE, refiners, tanker stocks), rattles Gulf equity markets, and introduces a genuine supply-disruption premium into oil at a moment when Iranian exports are already at zero and shipping costs are already described elsewhere in this feed as 'soaring' — so the setup, structurally, is not great.

headlines.title: The latest inflation data is expected to show price increases are accelerating
headlines.summary: September CPI is expected to print at 3.6% year-over-year and +0.6% month-over-month (which, if you're keeping score at home, is the kind of number that makes the Fed's 'one more hike and then we'll see' posture feel less like a plan and more like a prayer), and this is dropping into a market that is already dealing with 7.5% mortgage rates, a Bullard who sees 'two hikes and hope,' and a NY Fed president publicly disagreeing with traders about 2027 — so the rate-path uncertainty is genuinely unresolved. Affects SPY, TLT, rate-sensitive sectors (homebuilders, banks, utilities), and basically everything with a duration.

headlines.title: US chip stocks extend slide as China memory report, AI spending jitters hit sector - Reuters
headlines.summary: The semiconductor selloff is now a multi-session, multi-geography event (Nikkei down 2.6%, Micron -3.9%, AMD -2.3%, Broadcom -1.9%, Nvidia -1.3%) driven by the twin anxieties of Chinese memory competition and a growing suspicion that AI capex may be peaking — which is a somewhat awkward thing to believe simultaneously with ASML reporting that customers are placing orders through 2030, but markets have never been accused of excessive internal consistency. NVDA, AMD, MU, AVGO, and the SOX index are all in the blast radius, and given that semis have been the primary engine of the S&P's gains, a sustained rotation out of the sector is the kind of thing that turns a 'critical juncture' (per the CNBC headline also in this feed) into something less pleasant.
